content: Catuaba refers to infusions made from the bark of various trees native to Brazil. The most commonly used barks are obtained from the trees Trichilia catigua and Erythroxylum vacciniifolium. Other catuaba preparations may utilize the bark of trees belonging to genera or families such as Anemopaegma, Ilex, Micropholis, Phyllanthus, Secondatia, Tetragastris, and species within the Myrtaceae family. Although it is often claimed that catuaba is derived from the tree Erythroxylum catuaba, this species was described only once in 1904, and it is currently unclear to which tree this name originally referred. As a result, Erythroxylum catuaba is not recognized as a valid species (Kletter et al., 2004). Locally, catuaba is also known by other names, including Chuchuhuasha, Tatuaba, Pau de Reposta, Piratancara, and Caramuru. A commercial liquid preparation called Catuama contains multiple ingredients, one of which is catuaba derived from Trichilia catigua. In traditional Brazilian medicine, an infusion of catuaba bark is used as an aphrodisiac and a central nervous system stimulant. However, these claims have not been substantiated by rigorous scientific studies. Despite this, a journalist for the Discovery Channel has reported that scientific journals and conference presentations have supported its use for sexual enhancement. Catuaba contains a group of three alkaloids, named catuabine A, B, and C, which are thought to enhance sexual function by stimulating the nervous system. A study conducted by Manabe et al. in 1992 demonstrated that extracts from Trichilia catigua were effective in preventing potentially fatal bacterial infections and HIV infection in mice. Catuaba bark and its preparations are widely marketed as aphrodisiacs and treatments for erectile dysfunction, and they are available in health food stores and through online retailers.
